patterns.title: "-ment" on an adjective: the -ly word
patterns.explanation: Add -ment to an adjective to say how something is done, like English -ly. If you hear a word ending in -ment after a verb, it often means "in this way".
patterns.tip: Add -ment to the feminine form: lente → lentement, douce → doucement.

patterns.title: "-er" makes the verb
patterns.explanation: Add -er (or just -r after an -e) to a noun to get the verb for doing it. Many French verbs end in -er, so a noun you know can turn into a verb you can use.
patterns.tip: These verbs are regular -er verbs: je danse, tu danses, nous dansons.

patterns.title: "-eur", "-ier": the person who does it
patterns.explanation: Replace the verb ending with -eur, or add -ier to a noun, to name the person who does that thing or job. Listen for -eur or -ier at the end of job words.

patterns.title: "in-", "im-", "mé-": the opposite
patterns.explanation: Put in-, im- or mé- in front of a word to make it mean "not". Use im- before p, b and m.
patterns.tip: The gender stays the same: l'égalité, l'inégalité (both feminine).

patterns.title: "se" + verb: doing it to yourself
patterns.explanation: Put se (me, te, se...) before a verb when you do the action to yourself. Sometimes the meaning changes a little: demander is to ask, se demander is to wonder.
patterns.tip: Before a vowel, se becomes s': s'excuser. In the past tense these verbs use être.

patterns.title: "-tion", "-ment": the noun for the action
patterns.explanation: Change a verb into a noun with -tion/-sion or -ment, often the same as English -tion or -ment. Words ending in -tion are usually easy to guess from English.
patterns.tip: -tion and -sion nouns are feminine (la décision). -ment nouns are masculine (le remboursement).

patterns.title: "-ée", "-ure": the noun for the act or result
patterns.explanation: Add -ée or -ure to a verb or noun to name the act, its result, or a stretch of time. Une soirée is a whole evening, une entrée is a way in.
patterns.tip: These nouns are almost always feminine: la soirée, l'arrivée, la peinture.

patterns.title: "-é": how you feel or the state it's in
patterns.explanation: Add -é to a noun or a verb stem to describe the state someone or something is in, like English -ed: stressed, closed, broken.
patterns.tip: Add -e for a woman or a feminine noun: fatiguée, la porte fermée. The sound does not change.

patterns.title: "-té", "-esse": the noun for a quality
patterns.explanation: Add -té or -esse to an adjective to name the quality itself: proud becomes pride, sad becomes sadness. -té often matches English -ty.
patterns.tip: These nouns are feminine: la liberté, la tristesse.

patterns.title: "-erie", "-ie": the shop or the place
patterns.explanation: Add -erie or -ie to a seller or a product to name the shop or building. On a street sign, -erie usually means a shop.
patterns.tip: These places are feminine: la boulangerie, la mairie.

patterns.title: "re-": again or back
patterns.explanation: Put re- (or r- before a vowel) in front of a word to mean doing it again or going back. Revenir is to come back, recopier is to copy out again.
patterns.tip: In au revoir, re- + voir means "until we see each other again".

patterns.title: Two words make one
patterns.explanation: Two short words can join into one new word. Split it into its parts to find the meaning: bon + jour is good day, lave + linge is washes laundry.
patterns.tip: Compounds with a hyphen often take le: le lave-linge. Family words keep the gender of the person: la grand-mère.
